The sentence, too, may be read either interrogatively or affirmatively: nay more, the verb <foreign xml:lang="el">βλέπετε </foreign>may be taken either in the imperative mood, or in the subjunctive. I am rather of opinion, however, that it is expressive of chiding, and that the Corinthians are reaproved, because they suffered their eyes to be dazzled with empty show. “You greatly esteem others who swell out with mighty airs of importance, while you look down upon me, because I have nothing of show and boasting.” For Christ himself contrasts the <hi type="italic">judgment that is according to appearance</hi> with <hi type="italic">righteous judgment</hi>. (<reference osisRef="Bible:John.7.24">John 7:24</reference>, and <reference osisRef="Bible:John.8.15">John 8:15</reference>.) Hence he reproves the Corinthians, because, contenting themselves with show, or appearance, they did not seriously consider, what kind of persons ought to be looked upon as the servants of Christ.<div eID="gen122427" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122429" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">If any one trusteth in himself</hi> — an expression that is full of great confidence, for he takes it, as it were, for granted, that he is so certainly a minister of Christ, that this distinction cannot be taken from him. “Whoever,” says he, “is desirous to be looked upon as a minister of Christ, must necessarily count me in along with himself.” For what reason? “<hi type="italic">Let him</hi>,” says he. “<hi type="italic">think for himself</hi>, for whatever things he may have in himself, that make him worthy of such an honor, the same will he find in me.” By this he hinted to them, that whoever they might be that reviled him, ought not to be looked upon as the servants of Christ. It would not become all to speak thus confidently, for it might certainly happen — nay, it happens every day, that they same claim is haughtily advanced by persons, that are of no reputation, and are nothing else than a dishonor to Christ. <note n="766"> <div sID="gen122430" type="x-p"/> "<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vn tas de garnement</foreign>;" — "A band of profligates."<div eID="gen122430" type="x-p"/> </note> Paul, however, affirmed nothing respecting himself but what he had openly given proof of by clear and sure evidences among the Corinthians. Now should any one, while destitute of all proof of the reality, recommend himself in a similar manner, what would he do but expose himself to ridicule? To<hi type="italic"> trust in one’s self</hi> is equivalent to assuming to one’s self power and authority on the pretext that he serves Christ, while he is desirous to be held in estimation.<div eID="gen122429" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.10.7" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122426" osisID="2Cor.10.7" type="section"/>
entries.bce146cf6f65ae1be117a1c0aa29a5bd14187219: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.10.8" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.10.8" sID="gen122431" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122432" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">8.</hi> <hi type="italic">For though I should boast more largely of my authority</hi>. It was a sign of modesty, that he put himself into the number of those, whom he greatly excelled. At the same time, he was not disposed to show such modesty, as not to retain his authority unimpaired. He accordingly adds, that he has said less than his authority entitled him to say; for he was not one of the ordinary class of ministers, but was even distinguished among the Apostles. Hence he says: “Though I should boast more, <hi type="italic">I should not be ashamed</hi>, for there will be good ground for it.” He anticipates an objection, because he does not fail to speak of his own glory, while at the same time he refrains from making farther mention of it, that the Corinthians may understand, that, if he boasts, it is against his will, as in truth the false Apostles constrained him to it; otherwise he would not have done so.<div eID="gen122432" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122433" type="x-p"/>By the term <hi type="italic">power</hi> he means — the authority of his Apostleship, which he had among the Corinthians for, through all the ministers of the word have the same office in common, there are nevertheless, degrees of honor. Now God had placed Paul on a higher eminence than others, inasmuch as he had made use of his endeavors for founding <note n="767"> <div sID="gen122434" type="x-p"/> "<foreign xml:lang="fr">Pour fonder et batir</foreign>;" — "For founding and building up."<div eID="gen122434" type="x-p"/> </note> that Church, and had in many ways put honor upon his Apostleship. Lest, however, malevolent persons should stir up odium against him, on the ground of his making use of the term <hi type="italic">power</hi>, he adds the purpose for which it was given him — the salvation of the Corinthians. Hence it follows, that it ought not to be irksome to them, or grievous, for who would not bear patiently, nay more, who would not love what he knows to be of advantage to him? In the mean time, there is an implied contrast between his power, and that in which the false apostles gloried — which was of such a nature that the Corinthians received no advantage from it, and experienced no edification. There can, however, be no doubt, that all the ministers of the word are also, furnished with <hi type="italic">power</hi>; for of what sort were a preaching of the word, that was without <hi type="italic">power</hi>? Hence it is said to all —<div eID="gen122433" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122435" type="x-p"/>He that heareth you, heareth me;<lb/> he that rejecteth you, rejecteth me. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Luke.10.16">Luke 10:16</reference>.)<div eID="gen122435" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122436" type="x-p"/>As however, many, on false grounds, claim for themselves what they have not, we must carefully observe, how far Paul extends his <hi type="italic">power</hi> — so as to be to the edification of believers. Those, then, who exercise <hi type="italic">power</hi> in the way of destroying the Church, prove themselves to be tyrants, and robbers — not pastors. In the <hi type="italic">second</hi> place, we must observe, that he declares, that it was given to him by God. He, therefore, that is desirous to have any thing in his power to do, must have God as the Author of his power. Others, it is true, will boast of this also, as the Pope with full mouth thunders forth, that he is Christ’s vicar. But what evidence does he give of this? <note n="768"> <div sID="gen122437" type="x-p"/> "<foreign xml:lang="fr">Mais que fait-il? Quel tesmoignage en rend-il, pour luy adiouster foy</foreign>;" — "But what does he do? What proof does he give of it, that credit may be given him?"<div eID="gen122437" type="x-p"/> </note> For Christ has not conferred <hi type="italic">power</hi> of this kind upon dumb persons, but upon the Apostles, and his other ministers, that the doctrine of his Gospel might not be without defense. Hence the whole <hi type="italic">power</hi> of ministers is included in the word — but in such a way, nevertheless, that Christ may always remain Lord and Master. Let us, therefore, bear in mind, that in lawful authority these two things are required — that it be given by God, and that it be exercised for the welfare of the Church. It is well known, who they are, on whom God has conferred this <hi type="italic">power</hi>, and in what way he has limited the power he has given. Those exercise it in a proper manner, who faithfully obey his commandment.<div eID="gen122436" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122438" type="x-p"/>Here, however, a question may be proposed. “God says to Jeremiah,<div eID="gen122438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122439" type="x-p"/>Behold, I set thee over the nations, and kingdoms, <lb/> to plant, and to pluck up, to build and to destroy.<lb/> (<reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.1.10">Jeremiah 1:10</reference>.)<div eID="gen122439" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122440" type="x-p"/>We have, also, found it stated a little before, (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.10.5">2 Corinthians 10:5</reference>) that the Apostles were set apart on the same footing — that they might destroy every thing that exalted itself against Christ. Nay more, the teachers of the gospel cannot build up in any other way, than by destroying the old man. Besides, they preach the gospel to the condemnation and destruction of the wicked.” I answer that, what Paul says here, has nothing to do with the wicked, for he addresses the Corinthians, to whom he wished his Apostleship to be beneficial. With regard to them, I say, he could do nothing but with a view to edification. We have already observed, also, that this was expressly stated, that the Corinthians might know, that the authority of this holy man was not assailed by any one but Satan, the enemy of their salvation, while the design of that authority was their edification.<div eID="gen122440" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122441" type="x-p"/>At the same time, it is in other respects true in a general way, that the doctrine of the gospel has in its own nature a tendency to <hi type="italic">edification</hi> — not to <hi type="italic">destruction</hi>. For as to its destroying, that comes from something apart from itself — from the fault of mankind, while they stumble at the stone that was appointed form as a <hi type="italic">foundation</hi> (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Pet.2.8">1 Peter 2:8</reference>.) As to the fact, that we are renewed after the image of God by the destruction of the old man — that is not at all at variance with Paul’s words, for in that case destruction is taken in a good sense, but here in a bad sense, as meaning the ruin of what is God’s, or as meaning the destruction of the soul — as if he had said, that his <hi type="italic">power</hi> was not injurious to them, for instead of this the advantage of it for their salvation was manifested.<div eID="gen122441" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.10.8" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122431" osisID="2Cor.10.8" type="section"/>

9 That I may not seem to terrify. Again he touches on the calumny which he had formerly refuted, (2 Corinthians 10:2,) that he was bold in his writings, while in their presence his courage failed him. On this pretext they disparaged his writings.
"Ils rendoyent ses ecrits contemptibles;" — "They made his writings contemptible."
“What!” Said they, “will he terrify us by letters when at a distance, while, if present with us, he would scarcely venture to mutter a word!” Lest, therefore, his letters should have less weight, he answers, that no objection is advanced against him, that should either destroy or weaken his credit, and that of his doctrine, for deeds were not to be less valued than words. He was not less powerful in actions when present, than he was by words when absent. Hence it was unfair, that his bodily presence should be looked upon as contemptible. By deed, here, he means, in my opinion, the efficacy and success of his preaching, as well as the excellences that were worthy of an Apostle, and his whole manner of life. Speech, on the other hand, denotes — not the very substance of doctrine, but simply the form of it, and the bark, so to speak: for he would have contended for doctrine with greater keeness. The contempt, however, proceeded from this — that he was deficient in that ornament and splendor of eloquence, which secures favor.
"Par laquelle on acquiert grace enuers les hommes;" — "By which they acquire favor among men."
2 Corinthians 10:12-18
12. For we dare not make ourselves of the number, or compare ourselves with some that commend themselves: but they measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves among themselves, are not wise.
12. Non enim audemus nos quibusdam inserere aut comparare, qui se ipsos commendant: verum ipsi in se ipsis se metientes, et se ipsos comparantes sibi, non sapiunt.
13. But we will not boast of things without our measure, but according to the measure of the rule which God hath distributed to us, a measure to reach even unto you.
13. Nos autem non sine modo gloriabimur, sed pro mensura regulae, quam nobis distribuit Deus: mensura, inquam, perveniendi etiam usque ad vos.
14. For we stretch not ourselves beyond our measure, as though we reached not unto you: for we are come as far as to you also in preaching the gospel of Christ:
14. Non enim quasi ad vos non perveniremus, supra modum extendimus nos ipsos: siquidem usque ad vos pertigimus in Evangelio Christi.
15. Not boasting of things without our measure, that is, of other men’s labours; but having hope, when your faith is increased, that we shall be enlarged by you according to our rule abundantly,
15. Non gloriantes sine modo in alienis laboribus,
“Ne nous glorifians point outre mesure es labeurs d’autres, ou, Ne nous glorifians point en ce qui n’est point de nostre mesure, c’est d dire,” etc.; — “Not boasting beyond measure in the labors of others, or, not boasting in what is not within our measure, that is to say,” etc.
spem autem habentes, crescente fide vestra in vobis, nos magnificatum iri secundum nostram regulam in exuberantiam.
16. To preach the gospel in the regions beyond you, and not to boast in another man’s line of things made ready to our hand.
16. Ut etiam ultra vos evangelizem, non in aliena regula, ut de iis, quae parata sunt, glorier.
17. But he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.
17. Caeterum qui gloriatur in Domino glorietur.
18. For not he that commendeth himself is approved, but whom the Lord commendeth.
18. Non enim qui se ipsum commendat, ille probatus est: sed quem Dominus commendat.

12. For we dare not. He says this by way of irony, for afterwards he does not merely compare himself boldly with them, but, deriding their vanity, he leaves them far behind him. Now by this irony he gives a stroke, not merely to those foolish boasters,
Thrasones. — See vol. 1, p. 98, n. 1.
but also to the Corinthians, who encouraged them in their folly by their misdirected approbation. “I am satisfied,” says he, “with my moderate way; for I would not dare to put myself on a footing with your Apostles, who are the heralds of their own excellence.” In the mean time, when he intimates that their glory consists of mere speaking and boasting, he shows, how silly and worthless they are, while he claims for himself deeds instead of words, that is, true and solid ground of glorying. He may seem, however, to err in the very thing for which he reproves others, for he immediately afterwards commends himself. I answer, that his design must be taken into view, for those do not aim at their own commendation, who, entirely free from ambition, have no desire but to serve the Lord usefully.
“Car ceux qui estans vuides de toute ambition, desirent seulement de seruir a Dieu auec fruit et proufit, ne regardent point a se priser euxmesmes;” — “For those who being void of all ambition, simply desire to serve God with advantage and profit, have no view to exalt themselves.”
As to this passage, however, there is no need of any other explanation than what may be gathered from the words themselves, for those are said to commend themselves, who, while in poverty and starvation as to true praise, exalt themselves in vain-glorious boasting, and falsely give out, that they are what they are not. This, also, appears from what follows.
But they measure themselves by themselves Here he points out, as with his finger their folly. The man that has but one eye sees well enough among the blind: the man that is dull of hearing hears distinctly enough among the totally deaf. Such were those that were satisfied with themselves, and showed themselves off among others, simply because they did not look to any that were superior to themselves, for if they had compared themselves with Paul, or any one like him, they would have felt constrained to lay aside immediately that foolish impression which they entertained, and would have exchanged boasting for shame.
For an explanation of this passage we need look no farther than to the monks; for as they are almost all of them the most ignorant asses, and at the same time are looked upon as learned persons, on account of their long robe and hood, if any one has merely a slight smattering of elegant literature, he proudly spreads out his feathers like a peacock — a marvelous fame goes abroad respecting him — among his companions he is adored
“The principal places in the public schools of learning were filled very frequently by monks of the mendicant orders. This unhappy circumstance prevented their emerging from that ignorance and darkness which had so long enveloped them; and it also rendered them inaccessible to that auspicious light of improved science, whose salutary beams had already been felt in several of the European provinces. The instructors of youth, dignified with the venerable titles of Artists, Grammarians, Physicians, and Dialecticians, loaded the memories of their laborious pupils with a certain quantity of barbarous terms, arid and senseless distinctions, and scholastic precepts delivered in the most inelegant style, and all such that could repeat this jargon with a certain readiness and rapidity were considered as men of uncommon eloquence and erudition. The whole body of the philosophers extolled Aristotle beyond all measure, while scarcely any studied him, and none understood him.” — Mosheim’s Ecclesiastical History, (Lond. 1825,) volume 4 — Ed.
Were, however, the mask of the hood laid aside,
“Laisser derriere ceste masque de frocs et coqueluches;” — “To leave behind that mask of frocks and cowls.”
and a thorough examination entered upon, their vanity would at once be discovered. Why so? The old proverb holds good: “Ignorance is pert.”
“Our author quotes the same proverb in vol. 1, p. 460; and also when commenting on 1 Timothy 1:7 — Ed.
But the excessively insolent arrogance of the monks
“Ceste arrogance intolerable des moines;” — “This intolerable arrogance of the monks.”
proceeds chiefly from this — that they measure themselves by themselves; for, as in their cloisters there is nothing but barbarism,
“Pure barbaric et bestise;” — “Mere barbarism and stupidity.”
it is not to be wondered, if the man that has but one eye is a king among the blind. Such were Paul’s rivals, for inwardly they flattered themselves, not considering what virtues entitled a person to true praise, and how far short they came of the excellence of Paul, and those like him. And, certainly, this single consideration might justly have covered them with shame, but it is the just punishment of the ambitious, that by their silliness they expose themselves to ridicule, (than which there is nothing that they are more desirous to avoid,) and in place of glory, which they are immoderately desirous of,
“Laquelle ils appetent par moyens real propres;” — “Which they aim at by improper means.”
they incur disgrace.
entries.98bec8a9792709152ee371a7ad087b7c4c786e71: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.10.13" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.10.13" sID="gen122476" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122477" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">13.</hi> <hi type="italic">But we will not boast beyond our measure</hi> He now contrasts his own moderation with the folly of the false Apostles, <note n="780"> <div sID="gen122478" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Il oppose maintenant sa modestie a la sotte outrecuidance des faux apostres</foreign>;” — “He now contrasts his modesty with the foolish presumption of the false Apostles.”<div eID="gen122478" type="x-p"/> </note> and, at the same time, he shows what is the true measure of glorying — when we keep within the limits that have been marked out for us by the Lord. “Has the Lord given me such a thing? I shall be satisfied with this measure. I shall not either desire or claim to myself any thing more.” This he calls the <hi type="italic">measure of his rule.</hi> <note n="781"> <div sID="gen122479" type="x-p"/> “Within the measured and determinate limits of the stadium, the athletae were bound to contend for the prize, which they forfeited without hope of recovery, if they deviated even a little from the appointed course. In allusion to this inviolable arrangement, the Apostle tells the Corinthians: <hi type="italic">We will not boast of things without our measure, </hi>etc. It may help very much to understand this and the following verses, if, with Hammond, we consider the terms used in them as <hi type="italic">agonistical. </hi>In this view of them, the ‘measure of the rule’ (<foreign xml:lang="el">τὸ μέτρον τοῦ κανόνος)</foreign> alludes to the path marked out, and bounded by a white line, for racers in the Isthmian games, celebrated among the Corinthians; and so the Apostle represents his work in preaching the gospel as his spiritual race, and the province to which he was appointed as the compass or stage of ground, which God had distributed or measured out (<foreign xml:lang="el">ἐμέρισεν αὐτῳ)</foreign> for him to run in. Accordingly, ‘to boast without his measure,’ (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.10.13">2 Corinthians 10:13</reference>, <foreign xml:lang="el">εἰς τὰ ἄμετρα)</foreign> and to ‘stretch himself beyond his measure,’ (<foreign xml:lang="el">ὑπερεκτείνεσθαι)</foreign> refer to one that ran beyond or out of his line. ‘We are come as far as to you’ (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.10.14">2 Corinthians 10:14</reference>, <foreign xml:lang="el">ἄχρι ὑμῶν ἐφθάσαμεν) </foreign>alludes to him that came foremost to the goal; and ‘in another man’s line’ (<reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.10.16">2 Corinthians 10:16</reference>, <foreign xml:lang="el">ἐν ἀλλοτρίῳ κανόνι) </foreign>signifies — ’in the province that was marked out for somebody else,’ in allusion to the line by which the race was bounded, each of the racers having the path which he ought to run chalked out to him, and if one stepped over into the other’s path he extended himself over his line.” — <hi type="italic">Paxton’s </hi>Illustrations (“Manners and Customs,” volume 2.) — Ed.<div eID="gen122479" type="x-p"/> </note> For every one’s rule, according to which he ought to regulate himself is this — God’s gift and calling. At the same time, it is not lawful for us to glow in God’s gift and calling on our own account, but merely in so far as it is expedient for the glory of him, who is so liberal to us with this view — that we may acknowledge ourselves indebted to him for everything. <note n="782"> <div sID="gen122480" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Afin que nons luy facions hommage de tout ce que nons avons, confessans le tenir de luy</foreign>;” — “That we may make acknowledgment to him as to every thing that we have, confessing that we hold it from him.”<div eID="gen122480" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen122477" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122481" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">A measure to reach.</hi> By this clause he intimates, that he stands in no need of commendations expressed in words among the Corinthians, who were a portion of his glow, as he says elsewhere, (<reference osisRef="Bible:Phil.4.1">Philippians 4:1</reference>,) <hi type="italic">ye are my crown. </hi>He carries out, however, the form of expression, which he had previously entered upon. “I have,” says he, “a most ample field for glorying, so as not to go beyond my own limits, and you are one department of that field.” He modestly reproves, however, their ingratitude, <note n="783"> <div sID="gen122482" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Or en parlant ainsi, il taxe (modestement toutesfois) leur ingratitude</foreign>;” — “But by speaking thus he reproves, (modestly, however,) their ingratitude.”<div eID="gen122482" type="x-p"/> </note> in overlooking, in a manner, his apostleship, which ought to have been especially in estimation among them, on the ground of God’s commendation of it. In each clause, too, we must understand as implied, a contrast between him and the false Apostles, who had no such approbation to show.<div eID="gen122481" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.10.13" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122476" osisID="2Cor.10.13" type="section"/>
entries.114fa249cf45c5a8a3c34224284b485a90eb2f67: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.10.14" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.10.14" sID="gen122483" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122484" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">14.</hi> <hi type="italic">For we do not overstretch.</hi> He alludes to persons who either forcibly stretch out their arms, or raise themselves up on their feet, when wishing to catch hold of what is not at their hand, <note n="784"> <div sID="gen122485" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="el">Εκτείνω </foreign>is to extend, to stretch himselfe to the full of his measure: <foreign xml:lang="el">ὑπερεκτείνω,</foreign> to stretch himselfe beyond it, — to tenter himself far beyond his scantling.” — <hi type="italic">Leigh’s </hi>Critica Sacra. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen122485" type="x-p"/> </note> for of this nature is a greedy thirst for glory, nay more, it is often more disgusting. For ambitious persons do not merely stretch out their arms and lift up their feet, but are even carried headlong with the view of obtaining some pretext for glorying. <note n="785"> <div sID="gen122486" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Courent a bride auallee, et sont comme transportez a pour chasser quelque couleur de re glorifier</foreign>;” — “They run with a loose bridle, and are, as it were, hurried forward with the view of obtaining some pretext for glorying.”<div eID="gen122486" type="x-p"/> </note> He tacitly intimates that his rivals were of this stamp. He afterwards declares on what ground he had come to the Corinthians — because he had founded their church by his ministry. Hence he says, <hi type="italic">in the gospel of Christ; </hi>for he had not come to them empty, <note n="786"> <div sID="gen122487" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Vuide ne despourueu</foreign>;” — “Empty nor unprovided.”<div eID="gen122487" type="x-p"/> </note> but had been the first to bring the gospel to them. The preposition <hi type="italic">in</hi> is taken by some in another way; for they render it, <hi type="italic">by </hi>the gospel, and this meaning does not suit ill. At the same time, Paul seems to set off to advantage his coming to the Corinthians, on the ground of his having been furnished with so precious a gift.<div eID="gen122484" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.10.14" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122483" osisID="2Cor.10.14" type="section"/>
entries.97023ce8a0dd25eea06590a34c8b817082e73ba8: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.10.15" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.10.15" sID="gen122488" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">15.</hi> <hi type="italic">In the labors of others.</hi> He now reproves more freely the false Apostles, who, while they had put forth their hand in the reaping of another man’s harvest, had the audacity at the same time to revile those, who had prepared a place for them at the expense of sweat and toil. Paul had built up the Church of the Corinthians — not without the greatest struggle, and innumerable difficulties. Those persons afterwards come forward, and find the road made and the gate open. That they may appear persons of consequence, they impudently claim for themselves what did not of right belong to them, and disparage Paul’s labors.<div eID="gen122489" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122490" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">But having hope.</hi> He again indirectly reproves the Corinthians, because they had stood in the way of his making greater progress in advancing the gospel. For when he says that he hopes that, when <hi type="italic">their faith is increased</hi> the boundaries of his glowing will be enlarged, he intimates, that the weakness of faith under which they labored was the reason, why his career had been somewhat retarded. “I ought now to have been employed in gaining over new Churches, and that too with your assistance, if you had made as much proficiency as you ought to have done; but now you retard me by your infirmity. I hope, however, that the Lord will grant, that greater progress will be made by you in future, and that in this way the glory of my ministry will be increased according to the rule of the divine calling.” <note n="787"> <div sID="gen122491" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Selon la regle et mesure de la vocation Diuine</foreign>;” — “According to the rule and measure of the Divine calling.”<div eID="gen122491" type="x-p"/> </note> To <hi type="italic">glory in things that have been prepared</hi> is equivalent to <hi type="italic">glorying in the labors of others; </hi>for, while Paul had fought the battle, <hi type="italic">they </hi>enjoyed the triumph. <note n="788"> <div sID="gen122492" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Car combien que S. Paul eust guerroye, toutesfois les autres triomphoyent; c’est t dire, combien qu’il eust soustenu tout le fais et la peine, les autres en raportoyent la gloire</foreign>;” — “For although Paul had fought the battle, yet others enjoyed the triumph: that is to say, though he had borne all the burden and trouble, others carried off the glory.”<div eID="gen122492" type="x-p"/> </note><div eID="gen122490" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.10.15" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122488" osisID="2Cor.10.15" type="section"/>
entries.4f6203430545084b8fae51ab24fa06fed256627d: <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.10.17" annotateType="commentary" osisID="2Cor.10.17" sID="gen122493" type="section"/> <div sID="gen122494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">17.</hi> <hi type="italic">But he that glorieth</hi> This statement is made by way of correction, as his glorying might be looked upon as having the appearance of empty boasting. Hence he cites himself and others before the judgment-seat of God, saying, that those glory on good grounds, who are approved by God. To <hi type="italic">glory in the Lord, </hi>however, is used here in a different sense from what it bears in the first chapter of the former Epistle, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.1.31">1 Corinthians 1:31</reference>,) and in <reference osisRef="Bible:Jer.9.24">Jeremiah 9:24</reference>. For in those passages it means — to recognize God as the author of all blessings, in such a way that every blessing is ascribed to his grace, while men do not extol themselves, but glorify him alone. Here, however, it means — to place our glory at the disposal of God alone, <note n="789"> <div sID="gen122495" type="x-p"/> “<foreign xml:lang="fr">Eta ce qu’il en iugera</foreign>;” — “And according as he will judge of it.”<div eID="gen122495" type="x-p"/> </note> and reckon every thing else as of no value. For while some are dependent on the estimation of men, and weigh themselves in the false balance of public opinion, and others are deceived by their own arrogance, Paul exhorts us to be emulous of this glow — that we may please the Lord, by whose judgment we all stand or fall.<div eID="gen122494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen122496" type="x-p"/>Even heathens say, that true glory consists in an upright <hi type="italic">conscience.</hi> <note n="790"> <div sID="gen122497" type="x-p"/> “The heathens, though they could never attain to a true, spiritually sanctified, conscience, yet to live according to the natural dictates thereof, they accounted the only happiness, <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">Nil conscire sibi</hi></foreign> (<hi type="italic">To be conscious to one’s self of no crime, </hi>Hor. <reference osisRef="Bible:Eph.1.1 Bible:Eph.1.61">Ep. 1:1, 61</reference>,) was the only thing that made happy Pindar called it, <hi type="italic">the good nurse in our old age. </hi>So great a matter is it to have the testimony of a good conscience, void of offense, for that is <foreign xml:lang="la"><hi type="italic">mille testes</hi></foreign> — <hi type="italic">more </hi>than all the testimonies in the <hi type="italic">world.</hi>” — <hi type="italic">Burgesse </hi>on <reference osisRef="Bible:2Cor.1">2 Corinthians 1</reference>. — <hi type="italic">Ed.</hi><div eID="gen122497" type="x-p"/> </note> Now that is so much, but it is not all; for, as almost all are blind through excessive self-love, we cannot safely place confidence in the estimate that we form of ourselves. For we must keep in mind what he says elsewhere, (<reference osisRef="Bible:1Cor.4.4">1 Corinthians 4: 4</reference>,) that he is not conscious to himself of anything wrong, and yet is <hi type="italic">not thereby justified. </hi>What then? Let us know, that to God alone must be reserved the right of passing judgment upon us; for we are not competent judges in our own cause. This meaning is confirmed by what follows —<div eID="gen122496" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:2Cor.10.17" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen122493" osisID="2Cor.10.17" type="section"/>

For not he that commendeth himself is approved “For it is easy to impose upon men by a false impression, and this is matter of every day occurrence. Let us, therefore, leaving off all other things, aim exclusively at this — that we may be approved by God, and may be satisfied to have his approbation alone, as it justly ought to be regarded by us as of more value than all the applauses of the whole world. There was one that said, that to have Plato’s favorable judgment was to him worth a thousand.
The expression referred to occurs in the writings of Cicero. “Plato mihi unus est instar omnium;” — “Plato, even singly, is to me equal to all.” — (Cic. Brut. 51.) Cicero says elsewhere, that “he would rather err with Plato than think rightly with others.” — (Cic. Tusc. 1:17.) — Ed.
The question here is not as to the judgment of mankind, in respect of the superiority of one to another, but as to the sentence of God himself, who has it in his power to overturn all the decisions that men have pronounced.
CHAPTER 11
2 Corinthians 11:1-6
1. Would to God ye could bear with me a little in my folly: and indeed bear with me.
1. Utinam tolerassetis me paulisper in insipientia mea: imo etiam sufferte me.
“Mesme aussi supportez moy, ou, et certes vous me supportez;” — “Even so bear with me, or, and certainly you do bear with me.”
2. For I am jealous over you with godly jealousy: for I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ.
2. Nam zelotypus sum erga vos Dei zelo: adiunxi enim vos uni viro, ad exhibendam virginem castam Christo.
3. But I fear, lest by any means, as the serpent beguiled Eve through his subtilty, so your minds should be corrupted from the simplicity that is in Christ.
3. Sed metuo, ne qua fiat, ut quemadmodum serpens Evam decepit versutia sua: ita corrumpantur sensus vestri a simplicitate, quae est in Christo.
4. For if he that cometh preacheth another Jesus, whom we have not preached, or if ye receive another spirit, which ye have not received, or another gospel, which ye have not accepted, ye might well bear with him
4. Nam si is qui venit, (vel, si quis veniens,) alium Iesum praedicat, quem non praedicavimus; aut si alium Spiritum accipitis, quem non accepitis: aut Evangelium aliud, quod non accepistis, recte sustinuissetis.
5. For I suppose I was not a whit behind the very chiefest apostles.
5. Arbitror enim me nihilo inferiorem fuisse eximiis Apostolis.
6. But though I be rude in speech, yet not in knowledge; but we have been throughly made manifest among you in all things.
6. Caeterum licet imperitus sim sermone, non tamen scientia: verum ubique manifesti fuimus in omnibus erga vos.

<ns0:div xmlns:ns0="http://www.tei-c.org/ns/1.0" n="10" type="chapter">
               <ns0:head>CHAP. X.</ns0:head>
               <ns0:p n="1">1 NOw I Paul my self beseech you by the meek<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, and gentleness of Christ <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Meekness</ns0:hi> respecteth the Spirit or inward man, being a Ver<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tue that moderateth inward anger and rash passions. <ns0:hi>Gentleness</ns0:hi> more respecteth the outward conversation. The Apostle men<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tioneth both these Vertues, as eminent in Christ, who is our great Example, and to whom all Christians are bound to be conformable.</ns0:note>, who <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>in outward appearance.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> in presence <ns0:hi>am</ns0:hi> base among you <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He here repeateth the words of those who, in this Church, reproached him; they reported him a man, who, when he was there in presence with them, was lowly and humble enough:</ns0:note>, but being absent, am bold towards you <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">but when he was absent from them, then he wrote imperiously and confidently enough. The sense of the words is plainly this, I <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> (of whom some amongst you say, That when I am there with you I am low and humble enough, even to some degrees of baseness; but when I am ab<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sent, then I write like a Lord, boldly and confidently) I be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />seech you to consider the temper of our common Lord and Sa<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />viour, to remember how free he was from rash anger and passi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on, how gentle he was in his conversation, and by the obliga<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tion that is upon you, to love and practise those Vertues which you saw, or have heard of, in him.</ns0:note>.<ns0:note place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Hitherto the Apostle, (who in his former Epistle had blamed this Church for so many things, and dealt sharply with them) in this Epistle, hath treated them as if they had been a people that had had no <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>aults, or none but what in obedience to his former Epistle they had reformed, and become a new lump: which argueth, that the major part of the Members of it were a good and an obedient people, by whose prevalent Vote they had reformed much that was amiss. But in these four last Chapters, to let us know that there was yet some of the old leaven amongst them, he useth another stile; taking notice, that he understood there was amongst them another (though possibly the lesser) Party who had much vilified him; and justifying himself against their whisperings and ca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lumnies, not without some sharp reflections upon them.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="2">2 But I beseech you, that I may not be bold when I am present <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">It is true (saith the Apostle) when I have been with you, I have made it my business to behave my self with all obliging sweetness, not using that Authority which I might have used; and I beseech you, as not to blame me for that, (remembring the meekness and gentleness of Christ) so by your conversation not to force me to another kind of conversation amongst you; that you would not constrain me to a severer behaviour towards you when I am present with you,</ns0:note>, with that confidence where<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />with I think to be bold against some, which <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>reckon.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> think of us as if we walked according to the flesh <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">to be so free with some of you, as at present I am resolved to be; such, I mean, as have traduced me, as if I walked <ns0:hi>according to the flesh,</ns0:hi> that is, not guided by the holy Spirit of God, and the directions of his Word, but by some external, carnal considera<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ions, respecting my own profit, pleasure, or reputation, indulging my own pas<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sions or corrupt affections. <ns0:hi>Walking after the flesh</ns0:hi> is opposed to a <ns0:hi>walking after the Spirit,</ns0:hi> Rom. 8.1. He <ns0:hi>walketh after the flesh,</ns0:hi> to whom the fleshly appetite is the Principle, Rule, and End of his Actions: as he, on the contrary, to whom those habits of Grace, which are wrought in the Soul by the holy Spirit, or the Spirit himself more immediately by his motions or impulses, are the Principle of his Actions; and the Word dictated by the Spirit, is the Rule of his Actions; and the Glory of God is the End of his Actions, is truly said to <ns0:hi>walk after the Spirit.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="3">3 For though we walk in the flesh, we do not war after the flesh <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">There is a great difference betwixt <ns0:hi>walking in the flesh,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>warring after the flesh.</ns0:hi> The best of men in this life <ns0:hi>walk in the flesh,</ns0:hi> as their Souls are not in a state of separation from, but union with the body; but they do not <ns0:hi>walk after the flesh,</ns0:hi> as their fleshly appetite is not the Principle of their actions, nor the satisfaction of it the End of their actions. The Apostle, in the latter part of the Verse, changeth the Verb; in the former part he called our conversation, a <ns0:hi>Walking</ns0:hi>; in the latter part he calleth it a <ns0:hi>Warring</ns0:hi>; which he describeth Negatively in this Verse, Positively in the following<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>Verses. In calling it a <ns0:hi>War<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ring,</ns0:hi> he lets us know that it is, and will be a life of opposition, in which a Christian will have many Enemies: though his hand be against none, yet many hands will be against him. But though they be <ns0:hi>men of stri<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                           <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>e</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>contention,</ns0:hi> in a Passive sense, yet they are not so in an Active sense, according to the usual notion of warring: For they war <ns0:hi>not after the flesh,</ns0:hi> neither as <ns0:hi>fleshly men,</ns0:hi> nor in a carnal <ns0:hi>fleshly manner,</ns0:hi> nor yet for <ns0:hi>fleshly ends.</ns0:hi> The men of the World war for their honour and glory, or for re<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />venge and satisfaction of their lusts, or for the inlarging of their Territories and Dominions; but <ns0:hi>we do not thus war after the flesh.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note>:</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="4">4 (For the weapons of our warfare <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> not car<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nal <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">As our <ns0:hi>End</ns0:hi> is spiritual, so are our <ns0:hi>Means:</ns0:hi> the Means by which we manage our spiritual Fight, are spiritual. Whether by these <ns0:hi>Weapons</ns0:hi> he meaneth the Word of God, and his preach<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing the Gospel, or the Censures of the Church duly administred; it is true, they are not of a carnal nature, or fitted to the subduing of mens bodies, and bringing them into subjection; they are of a spiritual nature, and have their effects upon the mind and inward part of a man: yet</ns0:note>, but mighty <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>to God.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> through God, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Jer. 1.10.</ns0:note> to the pulling down of strong holds <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">through the concur<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rence of Divine Grace, there is in them a mighty force and power, to pull down <ns0:hi>strong Holds.</ns0:hi> By which Metaphorical ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pression he understands whatsoever opposeth the Gospel, and seemeth to defend and uphold men in their sinful courses; sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />duing the Will of man, which is so strong an Hold, that all the power of Hell cannot storm it.</ns0:note>.)</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="5">5 Casting down <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>
                  </ns0:note> imaginations <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, Reasonings;</ns0:note>, and every high thing that exalteth it self against the knowledge of God <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">and <ns0:hi>every high thing,</ns0:hi> every height of reasoning, <ns0:hi>which exalteth it self against the know<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ledge of God.</ns0:hi> The great Troublers of this Church of <ns0:hi>Corinth</ns0:hi> were the Heathen Philosophers, and such as had sucked in their Principles; with whose Notions, which were Conclusions drawn from Reason not sanctified and subdued to the Will of God, di<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />vers Doctrines of Faith would not agree. S. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> tells them, that the Gospel (which was the great weapon of his warfare) through the Power of God, was mighty to pull down the strong Holds, which Unbelief had in the carnal Understanding of men, to overthrow their Reasonings, the heights of them, which ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />alted themselves against the Doctrine of Faith.</ns0:note>, and bringing into captivity every thought to the obedience of Christ <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">And to bring <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, every thought or counsel into <ns0:hi>a captivity to the obedience of Christ</ns0:hi>; so as whatsoever was revealed by the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stles from the Spirit of God, men readily agreed and yielded obedience to; what-ever their thoughts or reasonings about it were, they gave credit to it: not because it appeared rational to them, but upon the divine authority of the Revelation; sub<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mitting their reason to that, and believing it the most rational thing in the World, that they should believe what God affirmed, and do what God commanded, and this blessed effect the Gos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel had in all those who heartily imbraced it: for indeed to give an assent to a Proposition, meerly upon a sensible or ra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tional demonstration, is no Faith; that is, no divine Faith; Truly to believe, in a divine sense, is to assent to a Proposition upon the credit of the Revelation, though we cannot make it out by our Reason: and this it is to have our thoughts brought into a Captivity to the Obedience of Christ. That whereas Reason, as it is since the Fall subjected in man, riseth up in Arms against several divine Propositions; and saith, <ns0:hi>How can these things be?</ns0:hi> How can one be three, and three one? How could the divine and humane nature unite in one person? How can the dead rise? <ns0:hi>&c.</ns0:hi> The Believer <ns0:hi>audit verbum Dei & tacet,</ns0:hi> readeth these things and others of the like nature plainly asser<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ted in holy Writ, and chides down his reason; resolving to give credit to these things meerly because God hath said them, who cannot ly. Thus our <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> thoughts, counsels, reasonings, deliberations, conclusions, all the product of our understand<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing, is brought into a Captivity to the Obedience of Christ; and reason it self, which is the Governess and Mistress of the Soul of man, is made a Captive to Revelation. And in this ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />peared the mighty power of the Weapons of the Apostles Warfare.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="6">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:469" />6 And having in readiness to revenge all disobe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dience, when your obedience is fulfilled <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">The Apostle certainly means by this, Excommunication; which was the <ns0:hi>Rod</ns0:hi> which he had before mentioned: asking them, if they would he should come unto them with a Rod; This Rod he here threatneth them with; telling them, that he had another Weapon of his warfare of a spiritual nature too, to be used against such as preferred themselves to be Believers, but walked disorderly; Only he at present spared them, be<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cause though a great part of them were obedient, yet there were some amongst them of whose Obedience he could not yet glory; but yet he hoped well, and therefore should wait, until by the use of all fair means (such as Exhortations, and Argu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments) he had reduced as many of them, as he could unto O<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bedience. But that being done, God had intrusted him with another Weapon, with which he would, in the name and by the authority of God, revenge his glory upon the disobedience of others. Herein the Apostle hath set a Rule and a Pattern to all Churches, where are multitudes that walk disorderly; not to be too hasty in Excommunicating them, but to proceed gradu<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ally; first using all fair means, and waiting with all patience for the reducing them to their duty, who will by any gentle, and fair means be reduced; and then revenging the honour and glory of God only upon such as will not be reclaimed.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="7">7 Do ye look on things after the outward ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pearance <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Are ye so weak as to judge of persons and things meerly from their Faces, pretences, or outward appearances? and to magnify these false Apostles and Teachers, meerly because they set forth, and magnify themselves, or because they take up a great breadth in the World, and live in a little state and splen<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />dor?</ns0:note>? <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 14.37. <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 4.6.</ns0:note> If any man trust to himself that he is Christs <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">If any of them do judge that he is the servant, or the Minister of Christ, why should he not think the same of me? what hath he to say to prove his relation to Christ more than I have? what hath he to glory in upon that account more than I have?</ns0:note>, let him of himself think this again, that as he <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> Christs, even so <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> we Christs <ns0:hi>p.</ns0:hi>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="8">8 For though I should boast somewhat more of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 13.10.</ns0:note> our authority (which the Lord hath given us for edification, and not for your destruction <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">Here is a remarkable Maxime, a Rule from which all Ec<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />clesiastical Superiours ought to measure their actions. <ns0:hi>God hath given to no Superiours a power for destruction of the Flock, but only for Edification</ns0:hi>; so as that no such can pretend to a power recei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ved from God, to do, or exact any thing which may any wayes hinder the Salvation of the Souls put under their trust; they ought to command or exact nothing, nor to do any thing, but what may probably tend to the promoting of peoples Faith, and Holiness, and Eternal Salvation. This Maxime the Apostle puts in in a <ns0:hi>parenthesis</ns0:hi> in this Verse, to sweeten what he had before spo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ken, concerning his readiness to revenge the disobedience of such who should appear to be stubborn and contumacious.</ns0:note>) <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">
                     <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 word">
                        <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap> 12.6.</ns0:note> I should not be ashamed <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">But he tells them, he should not be ashamed if he did boast some<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />thing more of a just and due authority than the false Apostles and Teachers had, who vi<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>ified him; for he was an Apostle, and had a more immediate authority than they who were ordinary Teachers.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="9">9 That I may not seem as if I would terrify you by letters <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">This was one imputation upon the Apostle (as we may learn by the next Verse.) I tell you (saith the Apostle) that I have an Authority, and a further Authority than those who vi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lify me can pretend unto: but I also tell you, I have no Autho<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rity to do any harm to any of you; all the Authority I have is for your Edification, as much as lyeth in me to promote the business of your Salvation; So that I need not be reported as one that went about to terrify you by my Letters; yet I know there are some who so represent me unto you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="10">10 For <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> letters (<ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Gr. <ns0:hi>saith he.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> say they) <ns0:hi>are</ns0:hi> weighty and powerful, but <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> bodily presence <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> weak, and <ns0:hi>his</ns0:hi> speech contemptible <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">There are some amongst you that tell you, that indeed (when absent) I write severely, and with authority; but when I am there with you, neither my behaviour, nor my speech, speaks any such Authority.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="11">11 Let such a one think this, that such as we are in word by letters when we are absent, such <ns0:hi>will we be</ns0:hi> also in deed when we are present <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">I would have no such person think so of me, for he shall find me the same in deed when I come, that I have spoke my self to be by my Letters. I do not write vainly, meerly to ter<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />rify you, but what I truly intend to do; and when I come he shall find that I will do.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="12">12 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 3.1. & 5.12.</ns0:note> For we dare not make our selves of the num<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ber, or compare our selves with some that com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mend themselves: but they measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves amongst themselves, are <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>under<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stand it not.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> not wise <ns0:note n="w" place="bottom">This whole Verse is a reflection upon the false Teachers of the Church of <ns0:hi>Corinth,</ns0:hi> from whose manners <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> purgeth him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self. I (saith he) dur<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>t no<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#PDCC" extent="1 letter">
                        <ns0:desc>•</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>, as some others, magnify my self, nor compare my self with those that do so. Neither is it any wisdom in them to contemn and despise others, in comparison of themselves; for observe, what measures they take, they only measure themselves by themselves, and compare themselves a<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mongst themselves, that is, with Birds of their own Feather, such as are like unto themselves, and of their own Faction and Party: which no wise men would do.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="13">13 But we will not boast of things without <ns0:hi>our</ns0:hi> measure, but according to the measure of the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>line</ns0:hi>
                     <ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g>
                  </ns0:note> rule which God hath distributed to us, a measure to reach even unto you.<ns0:note n="x" place="bottom">The Apostle may be understood, as speaking both of Spi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ritual gifts, and also of his Travails to the several places whither he had gone preaching the Gospel. He reflecteth still upon the false teachers who were crept into this Church; who (as it should seem) had much boasted of their gifts and abilities, and of their labours, and successes. In opposition to whom (he saith) that he boasted not <ns0:hi>without his measure,</ns0:hi> or (as it is in the <ns0:hi>Greek</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:gap reason="foreign">
                        <ns0:desc>〈 in non-Latin alphabet 〉</ns0:desc>
                     </ns0:gap>) <ns0:hi>unmeasurable things</ns0:hi>; but he kept himself within the <ns0:hi>measure of the rule</ns0:hi>; that is, according to that regular measure which God hath set us. Which <ns0:hi>measure</ns0:hi> extendeth even <ns0:hi>to you.</ns0:hi> You have those amongst you who boast unmeasurably of the gifts which they have, and of the great things which they do; I durst not do so (saith the Apostle) God hath given me <ns0:hi>a measure</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>a rule,</ns0:hi> according to that I have acted, and of those actings only I will glory. And in my so doing I can boast of <ns0:hi>you,</ns0:hi> for to you my <ns0:hi>measure</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>line</ns0:hi> hath reached. God hath made me an instrument to raise him up a Church amongst you.</ns0:note>
               </ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="14">14 For we stretch not our selves beyond <ns0:hi>our measure,</ns0:hi> as though we reached not unto you, for we are come as far as to you also, <ns0:hi>in preaching</ns0:hi> the Gospel of Christ <ns0:note n="y" place="bottom">For in our boasting of you as our Converts, amongst whom I have preached the Gospel, and God hath made my preaching successful; we do not stretch our selves beyond our measure, and arrogate that to our selves which belongeth not to us: for the thing is true, and ye know that in our preaching the Gospel we have come as far as unto you, and that God hath given our Labours success amongst you.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="15">15 Not boasting of things without <ns0:hi>our</ns0:hi> measure, <ns0:hi>that is,</ns0:hi> of <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 15.20.</ns0:note> other mens labours, but having hope, when your faith is increased, that we shall be <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>magnified in you.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> en<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />larged by you, according to our rule abundant<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ly <ns0:note n="z" place="bottom">So that although we have boasted of you, we have not boasted of things <ns0:hi>without our measure</ns0:hi>; that is of things that are not, or (as the Apostle expounds himself) of things that were not done by him but by other men; for his line did reach unto them, and his Labours had been imployed, and made successful amongst them. And he declares his hope, that when the Gos<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pel should have had its full success amongst them, and their <ns0:hi>faith</ns0:hi> should be <ns0:hi>increased</ns0:hi>; (either by the addition of more persons to the Church amongst them, or by the perfecting of their Faith, and other Graces;) they, who were Apostles and the Ministers of the Gospel to them, should by it be <ns0:hi>magnified,</ns0:hi> or made great: to wit by their means, who using much Navigation, would have opportunities to commend the Gospel, and the Ministry of it, to other people, amongst whom they should come: Wherein yet they should not exceed their <ns0:hi>Rule</ns0:hi>; for though ordinary Mi<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nisters be fixed in particular Churches and places, yet the Apo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />stles Rule was to go and preach the Gospel over the whole World, being tied to no certain people or places.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="16">
                  <ns0:pb facs="tcp:64193:470" />16 To preach the gospel in the <ns0:hi>regions</ns0:hi> beyond you <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">The Apostle here expoundeth what he meaneth by the term <ns0:hi>magnified</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>inlarged</ns0:hi> in the preceding verse, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> to have a door opened to preach the Gospel in places whither it was not yet come. God honoureth persons when he maketh them instru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments to bring any to an acquaintance with, and to the embra<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing of his Gospel, who formerly had been ignorant of it, and not acquainted with it.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> not to boast in another mans <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">Or, <ns0:hi>rule.</ns0:hi>
                  </ns0:note> line of things made ready to our hand <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">He here seemeth to reflect on the false Teachers crept into this Church, who had nothing to boast in but a pretended building upon other mens foundations, and carrying on a work by others made ready to their hands; and seemeth to prefer the work of Conversion, and an instrumenta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lity in that, before an instrumentality meerly in edification, and carrying on the work of God already begun in peoples Souls.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="17">17 <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Isa. 65.16. Jer. 9.24. 1 Cor. 1.31.</ns0:note> But he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">But we have none of us any thing to <ns0:hi>glory in</ns0:hi>; neither I <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> who plant, nor <ns0:hi>Apollos</ns0:hi> that watereth; whether God ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />keth use of us as the first Planters of the Gospel, or as Instru<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ments to carry on the work of the Gospel already planted, we have nothing of our own to <ns0:hi>glory in. God gives the increase</ns0:hi>; we have therefore no reason to glory in our selves, or in our own performances, but only to give thanks to God, who ma<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />keth use of us poor earthly Vessels to carry about and distribute that heavenly Treasure, by which he maketh Souls rich in Faith and good Works; all that we do is only instrumentally; God is all, and in all; as to primary Efficiency.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
               <ns0:p n="18">18 For, not he that commendeth himself, is ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />proved, but <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Rom. 2.29. 1 Cor. 4.5.</ns0:note> whom the Lord commendeth <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">
                     <ns0:hi>Solomon, Prov. 27.2.</ns0:hi> saith, <ns0:hi>Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth; a stranger, and not thy own lips.</ns0:hi> Self-commendation is an ungrateful sound to ingenuous ears; no man thinks another a jot the better for his commending him<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />self, but always hath the worser opinion of him for such boast<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing; but this Text speaketh of an higher approbation, <ns0:hi>viz.</ns0:hi> from God. No man is approved of God for his speaking well of himself; the business is, who they are who approve them<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />selves in the work which God hath committed to them; to whom the Lord will say, <ns0:hi>Well done, good and faithful servants:</ns0:hi> to whom the Apostle refers both himself, and those who magni<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />fied themselves, but vilified him.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
